title: Fish Schools May Follow One Neighbor at a Time
mediaSource: glassfish school synchronized swimming, transparent fish schooling, fish behavior experiment virtual reality

scenes.title: How do hundreds of fish turn together?
scenes.narration: When hundreds of fish turn at once, it looks like the whole school is thinking together. But a recent study suggests the rule behind it may be surprisingly simple.
keywords: glassfish school synchronized swimming underwater real photo

scenes.title: They may not track the whole group
scenes.narration: Scientists often assumed fish align with the average direction of several nearby neighbors. In glassfish, researchers found that an individual may instead copy one nearby fish at a time.

scenes.title: One quick copy after another
scenes.narration: When one fish finishes a turn, a brief window opens for another fish to match that movement. Mature glassfish react very quickly, creating a chain of coordinated turns through the group.

scenes.title: Virtual fish tested the idea
scenes.narration: The team also placed real glassfish in a virtual reality setup with simulated fish. When the virtual fish changed direction, the real fish responded in the way the one-neighbor model predicted.

scenes.title: Simple rules can build a huge school
scenes.narration: The key is that no central leader is required. A simple rule of rapidly responding to one neighbor can be enough to create the complex movement of an entire fish school.
keywords: large fish school coordinated movement underwater

scenes.title: Follow one fish, move as a crowd
scenes.narration: A school may look like hundreds of animals making one decision at the same moment. In reality, that spectacular motion may emerge from many tiny one-to-one reactions happening in sequence.
